text: (title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) There is a need for a better understanding of the mode-of-action of exogenous fibrolytic enzymes (EFE) used as additives in ruminant feeds.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Four forages, treated with EFE, were evaluated in vitro and histologically, in an attempt to determine the effect of EFE on tissue degradation.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Weeping love grass, kikuyu leaf material, lucerne and wheat straw stem material were histologically evaluated.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Simultaneously, milled samples were incubated in the rumen fluid inoculated media for the determination of in vitro digestibility.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The main focus, however, was a quantitative assessment of the degradation of the plant tissue at histological level over a 24 h incubation period.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Degradation of cell wall components were quantified using the image analysis software.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) After 12 h of incubation, cell walls of the metaxylem of kikuyu and weeping love grass leaf material were thinner for the EFE treatment than for the control treatment.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Treatment also resulted in a significant thinning effect of the cell walls of kikuyu phloem (12 h) and the adaxial epidermis (24 h).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The abaxial epidermis at 12 h was thinner for weeping love grass due to EFE treatment.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) For stem material, a thinning of the epidermis of EFE treated lucerne was observed.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Histological findings were concomitant with higher in vitro digestibilities of EFE treated lucerne and kikuyu.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) It was concluded that image analysis can be useful to quantify changes in cell wall due to the treatment of forages with EFE.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) There was a definite, subtle thinning effect of EFE on cell wall thickness of plant material which could be indicative of the mode-of-action of EFE.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Additives such as exogenous fibrolytic enzymes (EFE) have been researched worldwide.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Promising effects on DMI, digestibility, feed utilization and production in especially dairy cows and feedlot cattle have been demonstrated (Beauchemin et al., 2003; Eun et al., 2007).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) However, research also points to varied responses of ruminants to EFE treatment of their diets.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) A better understanding of the mode-of-action of EFE is of importance (Colombatto et al., 2003) as responses vary due to factors such as experimental conditions, dose rate of EFE, method of application, etc. (Beauchemin et al., 1995; 2003).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Forage heterogeneity contributes largely to the variation in degradability of plant material even with similar chemical composition but varied anatomy (Travis et al., 1997).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) It is thus important to recognize the botanical characteristics of plant material as a factor determining its nutritional value (Walters, 1971).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Research is limited on the effect of exogenous enzymes on forage tissue at the histological level, although some research points to the effect of EFE at the cellular level.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Recently, it has been reported that EFE alters the fibre structure of plant material (Giraldo et al., 2008).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The objectives of this study was to determine the effect of EFE on in vitro digestibility of kikuyu (Pennisetum clandestinum) hay, weeping love grass (Eragrostis curvula) hay, lucerne

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) For the histological investigation, leaf material of freshly cut weeping love grass (Eragrostis curvula) and kikuyu (Pennisetum clandestinum) and stem material of freshly cut lucerne (Medicago sativa) and wheat straw (Triticum) were collected and prepared for sectioning by infusion of tissue with tissue freezing medium (Cryo-M-Bed, embedding compound, Bright Instrument Company Ltd, Huntingdon, England) prior to cryofreezing in liquid nitrogen.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Cross sections (20 µm) were made on a cryostat and fixed to microscope slides (Lasec™) by means of clear double-sided tape, as described by Akin (1982).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Two slides (containing three sections each) were incubated back to back in 50 mL glass test tubes.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Two test tubes per treatment (EFE or Control) were allowed per incubation time and the whole experiment was duplicated.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Incubation times were 0 h (no incubation), 6 h, 12 h and 24 h in buffered rumen fluid.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The EFE was a dilution of 1 mL ABO 374 supernatant in 200 mL distilled water, of which 1 mL was added to each slide in the test tubes.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The ABO 374 supernatant contained xylanases (296 ± 0.07 U/mg protein), cellulases (1.44 ± 0.39 U/mg protein) and mannanases (1.10 ± 0.37 U/mg protein) as the major fibrolytic enzyme components (Cruywagen & Van Zyl, 2008).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Slides were pre-treated with EFE or distilled water for 12 h in glass tubes sealed with rubber stoppers prior to incubation in buffered rumen fluid.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) To the tubes containing the slides, 40 mL buffer (pH 6.8) and 10 ml filtered and blended rumen fluid was added under strict anaerobic conditions.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Rumen fluid was collected prior to the morning feeding from two cannulated sheep, filtered through four layers of cheesecloth and blended for 30 seconds before being added to the buffer.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Sheep were maintained on a lucerne hay and oat hay diet (50 : 50 mixture) and supplemented with 250 g/d of a commercial feed concentrate.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The tubes were sealed with rubber stoppers under CO 2 gas phase and incubated in a shaking water bath at 39 ºC. After the appropriate incubation periods, slides (two per treatment) were randomly removed from the test tubes, rinsed in ice cold water and stained with Toluidine blue for 5 minutes.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) They were subsequently rinsed and covered with a cover slip to prevent the sample from drying out.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Samples were observed on an Olympus Cell R system attached to an IX-81 inverted microscope equipped with a F-view-II cooled CCD camera (Soft Imaging Systems).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Images were acquired by using Olympus 40x (leaf material) and 4x objectives (stem material) and the Cell R imaging software.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The total magnification was 400x or 40x, respectively for leaf and stem material when the 10x ocular piece's magnification is calculated as well.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Images were analysed using the Cell R software (Olympus Biosystems GMBH, Muenster, Germany).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) In vitro digestibility was evaluated according to the method for ""In vitro true digestibility using the DAISY incubator"" as described by ANKOM Technology, Fairport, NY.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Samples were milled through a 1.5 mm screen and sieved before being weighed (0.5 g) into F57 filter bags.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Samples were then pre-treated with EFE as described earlier, or distilled water (control) for a period of 12 h prior to incubation in buffered rumen fluid.
(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Bags were removed and analysed after 24 h of incubation.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The in vitro digestibility data were subjected to a Factorial ANOVA, whereas histology data were analyzed with either a Bonferroni or Newman-Keuls multifactorial test, using Statistica 8.1 (2008).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The cell types observed and measured for cell wall thickness were the abaxial and adaxial epidermis, the metaxyleme, xyleme, phloem island cells and the parenchyma bundle sheath.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) These structures are presented in Figure 1 , using kikuyu and weeping love grass as examples.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) For the stem material, in addition to the cell wall thickness of the epidermis, the total tissue surface area was also determined.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) It can be seen in Figure 2 (using kikuyu leaf material as example) how the tissue structures of the Control and EFE treated specimens were degraded after 24 h of incubation in buffered rumen fluid.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The degradation of the plant tissues observed here is in agreement with the findings of Buxton & Readfearn (1997).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) These authors found that mesophyll was highly digestible, while parenchyma, collechyma and parenchyma bundle sheaths were moderately to highly digestible.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The structural components of epidermis, vascular tissue and schlerenchyma have low digestibilities, or can even be indigestible.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The cell wall thickness values and surface areas of the EFE and Control specimens following incubation were computed and the reduction in cell wall thickness and surface areas were determined.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The reduction in cell wall thickness was used as indication of the effect of EFE treatment on fibre digestion and is presented in resulted in thinner (P <0.05) adaxial epidermis (kikuyu 24 h) and abaxial epidermis (weeping love grass 12 h) values compared to the Control.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Treatment also decreased metaxylem cell wall thickness for both kikuyu and weeping love grass at 12 h of incubation.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Phloem cell walls were thinner only for kikuyu after 12 h incubation (P <0.05).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Metaxylem, expressed as a percentage surface area of the unincubated (0 h) kikuyu specimen, was also decreased by EFE treatment (P <0.05).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) For the stem material investigated (Table 2 ), the only significant observation (P <0.05) was a decrease in the epidermal cell wall thickness of lucerne at 12 h of incubation in buffered rumen fluid with EFE.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Overall, EFE resulted in a subtle reduction of cell wall thickness of the various tissues studied.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) This is based on the calculation of the percentage reduction in cell wall thickness from 0 h to 12 h and 24 h of the EFE treatment compared with the control.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) These findings support the hypothesis that EFE can degrade cell wall structures, thereby allowing ruminal microbes earlier access to fermentable substrate during the initial phase of digestion (Colombatto et al., 2003).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Should the cell wall structures be weakened or altered in such a way as to allow earlier access of microbes to the cell contents as proposed here, it follows that the digestibility could be positively influenced.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) This was observed in the current study (Figure 3 ) where the 24 h in vitro digestibility of kikuyu and lucerne was increased by EFE treatment.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) The in vitro digestibility of EFE treated lucerne hay (770.0 g/kg) was higher (P = 0.008) than that of the control (747.0 g/kg).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Similarly, EFE resulted in an increase in in vitro digestibility from 619.0 g/kg (Control) to 654.0 g/kg for the EFE treated kikuyu sample (P = 0.004).

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) No treatment effects on the digestibility of weeping love grass or wheat straw were observed.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Results from this study suggest that exogenous fibrolytic enzymes have a thinning effect on the cell wall components of plant material which was substantiated by improved in vitro digestibility of EFE treated samples.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) Although limited significant effects were reported in terms of cell wall thinning of the various tissues studied, the key to the observations were that subtle effects were indeed observed.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) This is in strong agreement with literature where effects on cell wall digestion have been proposed by several researchers as a contributing factor to the mode-of-action of EFE.

(title:Exogenous fibrolytic enzymes to unlock nutrients: Histological investigation of its effects on fibre degradation in ruminants) It was concluded that EFE altered fibre cell wall structures, thereby positively influencing fibre digestion.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) White-rot fungi are major degraders of woody materials in terrestrial environments because of their ability to decompose lignin.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) However, little is known on the possible associations of white-rot fungi with other microorganisms during wood decay.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) We investigated the numbers, community composition and functional traits of bacteria present in natural wood samples under advanced decay by the white-rot basidiomycete Hypholoma fasciculare.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The wood samples contained high numbers of cultivable bacteria (0.2-8 Â 10 9 colony forming units (CFU) per g of dry wood).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Most cultivable bacteria belonged to Proteobacteria and Acidobacteria (75% and 23% of sequences, respectively).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The same phyla were also found to be dominant (59% and 23%, respectively) using a non-culturable quantification technique, namely, direct cloning and sequencing of 16sRNA genes extracted from wood.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Bacteria that could be subcultured consisted of acid-tolerant strains that seemed to rely on substrates released by lignocellulolytic enzyme activities of the fungus.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) There were no indications for antagonism (antibiosis) of the bacteria against the fungus.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) White-rot basidiomycetes are important decomposers of woody materials in terrestrial ecosystems and have the unique ability to decompose all major wood polymers, namely, cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) This complete decomposition relies on the production of lignocellulose-degrading enzymes (Martı ´nez et al., 2005; Baldrian and Vala ´s ˇkova ´, 2008).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) As opposed to fungi, bacteria have only limited ability to degrade wood because their size limits penetration of woody cell walls and, moreover, they have restricted abilities to modify lignin (Hatakka, 2001; De Boer and van der Wal, 2008).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) In principle, fungal decay activities do provide opportunities for access and growth of bacteria, as the lignin barrier is weakened and easily degradable oligomers are released from wood polymers by fungal enzymes (De Boer et al., 2005; Baldrian, 2008).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The oligomers do, however, also form the energy substrates for the fungus.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Consequently, fungi may try to avoid proliferation of bacteria in wood, for example, by producing toxic secondary metabolites.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Indeed, Folman et al. (2008) showed that two white-rot fungal species, Hypholoma fasciculare and Resinicium bicolor, had strong bactericidal effects when they colonized beech woodblocks, and basidiomycetes were shown to affect the community composition of bacteria in soils (Tornberg et al., 2003; Warmink and van Elsas, 2008).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) As some recent reports demonstrate a high bacterial diversity in samples in natural decaying wood in forests (Mikluscak and Dawson-Andoh, 2004; Murray and Woodward, 2007; Zhang et al., 2008) , it is not clear whether the bactericidal activities of white-rot fungi do also continue during prolonged decay.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The aim of this study was to investigate the abundance, composition and properties of bacteria in natural wood samples that are in a stage of advanced decay by the white-rot basidiomycete H. fasciculare.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Wood samples were taken adjacent to fruiting bodies of H. fasciculare from deciduous wood resources as described in the Supplementary information.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Procedures for analysis of wood characteristics, fungal biomass (ergosterol), lignocelluloytic enzyme activities, enumeration of bacteria, cultivable and total bacterial community composition and physiological characteristics of bacterial isolates are given as Supplementary information.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Ergosterol content of the wood samples ranged from 80 to 314 mg per g of wood dry mass, corresponding approximately to 15-65 mg g À1 of fungal biomass (Ba ˚a ˚th, 2001).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The dominance of H. fasciculare in the fungal community of the wood samples was confirmed by DGGE analysis of the ITS region of fungal DNA.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The activity of extracellular lignocellulose-degrading enzymes was between 0-0.68 mU g À1 for laccase, 0.33-1.30 mU g À1 for Mnperoxidase, 1.4-5.7 mU g À1 for endoglucanase and 0.9-10.3 mU g À1 for endoxylanase demonstrating the active decomposition of all wood polymers by the fungus.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) All wood samples were strongly acidic, pH ranging from 3.6 to 4.3, and contained 0.2-7.8 Â 10 9 bacterial CFU per g of wood dry mass.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) This is several orders of magnitude higher than the numbers of bacteria that survive in wood after colonization by H. fasciculare (Folman et al., 2008).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Numbers of CFU were slightly, but significantly, higher on water-yeast agar (pH 5) than on TSB-agar (pH 5 or pH 6.5).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) A total of 134 partial ribosomal genes directly amplified from DNA extracted from the wood we sequenced.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) These ribosomal gene fragments were composed of 63 operational taxonomic units, defined as sequences with 497% identity.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The calculated values of the abundance-based richness estimators were 111 for S CHAO1 and 123 for S A w CE (see Supplementary information).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The phylogenetic relationships of clones with known bacterial isolates or environmental rDNA sequences are shown in Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 1.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The community was dominated (59% of the clones) by Proteobacteria, of which approximately half consisted of Alphaproteobacteria (Table 1 ).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Alphaproteobacteria clones were affiliated with the orders Sphingomonadales, Rhizobiales, Caulobacterales and Rhodospiralles.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Betaproteobacteria clones were largely represented by the genus Burkholderia, whereas Gammaproteobacteria clones fell into the orders Legionellales and Xanthomonadales.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The second most abundant group of clones (23%) clustered within the phylum Acidobacteria and the third (7%) belonged to the phylum Firmicutes.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Other phyla detected included Verrumicrobia, Bacteroidetes, Planctomycetes and TM7. The phylum Actinobacteria, whose members are known for their cellulolytic and lignin-modifying activities (Kirby, 2006) , were only present at low numbers which was the main contrast to the study of Zhang et al. (2008).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Identification of cultivable members of the wood bacterial community showed a similar dominance of Proteobacteria and Acidobacteria as for the clones (Table 1 ).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Multiple identical sequences were observed in Burkholderia sp. (13 sequences representing eight phylotypes), Xanthobacteriaceae (11 sequences representing eight phylotypes) and Acidobacteria isolates (11 representing four phylotypes).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Of the isolates that could be successfully cultured, all except one (Pedobacter sp. WH4) were able to grow at pH 4.0.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The Alpha-and Betaproteobacteria tested seemed to be metabolically versatile and could use several low molecular weight sugars that are released by extracellular fungal cellulases and hemicellulases.
(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) None of the isolates, however, was able to hydrolyze colloidal cellulose.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Small aromatic compounds, which are released on degradation of lignin, were less commonly used.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Interestingly, none of the isolates grew on oxalic acid, which is exuded by H. fasciculare.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Trehalose, a disaccharide used for carbon storage by fungi, and chitin, the component of fungal cell wall were not utilized either, although N-acetyl-D-glucosamine, the monomeric component of chitin, was used as a growth substrate by many strains (Table 2 ).

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Most Gammaproteobacteria failed to utilize any of the supplied substrates as a sole carbon source.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The isolates of Acetobacteraceae, Acidobacteriaceae bacterium, Burkholderia glathei, and one strain of each Caulobacteraceae, Rhodospirillaceae and Xanthomonadaceae failed to grow even when the medium was supplemented with yeast extract, pointing to specific nutritional requirements.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) None of the isolates exhibited in vitro antagonism against H. fasciculare.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) This is in line with a dependency of the bacteria on lignocellulolytic activities of the fungus.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) The relatively high abundance and diversity of bacteria in this study compared with that of Folman et al.(2008) could indicate that selective effects of the white-rot basidiomycete H. fasciculare on the bacterial community are stronger during initial decay than in its later phases.

(title:Phylogenetic composition and properties of bacteria coexisting with the fungus Hypholoma fasciculare in decaying wood) Another possibility is that bacteria, which are adapted to the harmful conditions created by the fungus, proliferate during prolonged decay.

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) To gain an improved understanding of the hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism, two-dimensional correlation infrared spectroscopy (2D-PCIS) was employed to analyze the functional group evolution in xylan chars between 200 and 600 °C, and through combination with the obtained volatiles releasing properties.

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) Simultaneously, the pathway of xylan decomposition was deduced to illustrate the pyrolysis mechanism.

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) The depolymerization and ring-opening reactions of xylan started at 200℃.

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) After that, it was mainly xylan matrix degradation reaction to form char structure which mainly consisted of phenyl rings and oxygen-containing cyclic compounds with aliphatic chains.

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) With temperature increasing (300-450 ℃), the decarbonylation reaction, removal of C]C and fatty chains reactions were intensified and the molecular structures of xylan char reconstructed to form fusedring compounds on the order of 1 × 2 and 2 × 2 through condensation.

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) Dehydrogenation and polycondensation reaction of xylan increased at higher temperature (450-600 °C).

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) The char structure was composed of high-order fused-ring compounds, and the production of H 2 and CH 4 increased greatly.

(title:Hemicellulose pyrolysis mechanism based on functional group evolutions by two-dimensional perturbation correlation infrared spectroscopy) Biomass, which is abundant, clean, and renewable, is considered a potential future solution to fossil fuel depletion and pollution as they can efficiently convert into gas, oil, and solid char products through pyrolysis.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) Agricultural residues are the most readily available source of lignocellulosic biomass in the world and, therefore, the materials of highest interest for the production of bio-fuels, chemicals, and polymeric materials.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) In China, an annual total of 700 million tons of agricultural residues are produced from rice, wheat, corn, and soybean, accounting for 20-30% of the world's total production.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) Because the crystalline structure of their remains is composed of hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin, it is very difficult to break down and degrade naturally.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) Most remaining straw or husk is destroyed, buried, or burned, resulting in resource waste and environmental pollution.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) Therefore, the question of how to use this resource effectively becomes more and more important  and biological pretreatments have the advantage of being less expensive and more environmentally friendly compared to mechanical, chemical, thermal, and thermo-chemical treatments.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) In recent years, researchers have begun to pay attention to various cellulose-degrading bacteria given their fast growth, expression of multienzyme complexes, and resistance to extreme environments.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) There have been many studies of cellulose-degrading bacteria and they mostly concentrate on mesophilic or thermophilic bacteria.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) Under low temperatures, the activity of microorganisms is weak; thus, in the colder regions of China, the initial stage temperature of composting cannot increase rapidly and agricultural residues are not quickly or effectively degraded.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) However, few studies have focused on cellulosedegrading bacteria under low-temperature conditions.

(title:Cellulose-Degrading Strains: their Screening and Application to Corn Straw in Low-Temperature Environments) The aims of this study were to: 1) isolate cellulosedegrading strains from the soil in a cold region of China, 2) directly apply the screened strains to corn straw under low temperatures and measure their degradation index, and 3) analyze their enzymatic properties to understand their potential value for applications.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Frost events are a major weather-related phenomenon impacting agriculture and sometimes causing devastating effects on crops.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Technically, frost refers to the ice crystals formed by freezing, but its meaning is also referred to describe a meteorological phenomenon characterized by falling air temperature below 0 • C.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Although crops are ready to defend themselves and are resistant to frosts in winter, food crops are vulnerable to below-freezing temperatures during the vegetative restart.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Frosts that occur during the active growth of crops are called late frosts and they are damaging for the sensitive tissues of plants such as shoots, flowers, and new leaves.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Late frosts are meteorological events characterized by low air temperature, less than or equal to 0 • C, and they cause lethal damages to the plants and huge economic losses, even if they generally only last a few hours.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Frost damages occur in all agricultural areas, affecting both temperate and tropical countries, and huge economic losses due to late frosts are observed worldwide.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) For example, in the USA, the fruit crop economic losses after April 2007 were 86 million USD and the losses caused by late frosts were greater than any other meteorological event.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Frosts can be distinguished in advective and radiative frosts. Late frosts, which affect the most important Italian agricultural areas, are mainly radiative frosts, but sometimes a combination of two categories of frosts occurs.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Radiative frosts are characterized by a temperature inversion through radiant exchange, which leads the energy loss resulting in soil and crops cooling.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) They usually occur in clear and calm nights with daily temperatures greater than 0 • C.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) On the other hand, advective frosts are characterized by an air temperature falling below 0 • C even during the day. They usually occur in windy and cloudy conditions and they are caused by cold air blows.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Since the first crops were grown, late frost damages have always represented a serious problem for humans.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) In fact, when late frosts occur, they can lead to total crop failures in only one night of freezing temperatures.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) So, many methods have been developed to protect crops from damages frost over time.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Frost protection is distinguished into active or direct methods and passive or indirect methods.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) The active or direct defense involves specific and temporary actions taken when freezing occurs in order to replace energy loss during the frost night; in fact, the active defense is carried out only with radiative frosts because weather conditions in advective frosts make impossible to implement ad hoc defense methods.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Active methods are characterized by shielding, dynamic, and thermal techniques.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) The oldest active defense techniques employ artificial fog to prevent the risk of late frosts.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) In fact, when the humidity in the air increases near the ground due to the artificial fog, the air shielding power enhances, hindering energy losses from the ground.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) The shielding devices make a smoke cloud by burning of organic materials at the crops level.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) The dynamic means rely on using wind machines to prevent the thermal inversion by air mixing.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) In fact, wind machines draw the warmer air from the upper air layers and push it down to the crops level resulting in soil and crops warming.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) The use of fans began from California in 1920 with a 12 m high tower at the top of which a fan with two propellers was located.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Among the dynamic techniques, helicopters are a high-efficacy means for large areas.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Finally, the thermal devices include heaters, which provide heat in order to warm up the air at crop level and sprinklers, which exploit the heat during a phase change from water to ice.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) The most commonly used thermal technique is frost-free irrigation, which is carried out with continuous rain and with over-or under-plant sprinklers, both for advective and radiative frosts.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) The over-plant irrigation produces ice crystals on shoots and young leaves, which keep the temperature more than 0 • C. Instead, ice crystals on the ground are formed with the under-plant irrigation.
(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) Among the under-plant sprinklers, micro-sprinklers are the most efficient ones.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) On the other hand, the passive or indirect defense involves preventive measures carried out before frost events, including ecological (e.g., site selection for crops and soil management) and biological (e.g., treatment with growth regulators and chemicals) techniques.

(title:Insulating Organic Material as a Protection System against Late Frost Damages on the Vine Shoots) However, the passive defense is mainly based on crop selection for timing of phenological development in order to minimize frost damage.
